passage: Note, student counselling, Thursday. Karthik, 20, asked for advice before Diwali. He does not believe in God but does not want to hurt his family, and his mother expects him at the puja. I asked what he wants. He said, "I want to be there, and I don't want to pretend." I did not tell him what to believe. We practised what he could say. On Monday he came back. He had told his mother in the kitchen, "Amma, I don't pray the way you do, but I'd love to sit with you and light the lamps." She was quiet, then handed him the matchbox. He said he felt nervous first, then warm. I asked whether he had been honest and still belonged. He said yes. I will check in after the holidays. Deepika, counsellor

qa.q: What did Karthik's mother do after he spoke in the kitchen?
qa.a: She was quiet, then handed him the matchbox.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel telling his mother, according to the note?
qa.a: Karthik felt nervous at first and then warm, since he could be honest and still belong.

qa.q: Which choice by Karthik kept honesty and belonging together?
qa.a: Karthik told his mother gently that he does not pray the way she does but would love to sit with her and light the lamps, without pretending faith.

qa.q: How might Karthik's mother have felt handing him the matchbox?
qa.a: Probably touched and accepting. After being quiet, she gave him a real part in the puja.

grounding: A non-believer joins a family puja for love and tradition without pretending faith, being gently open about it.

passage: Tuesday night. Went to Ajji's Ganesh puja today. I have never believed, and I told Ajji last year I'm not sure about God. She just said, "Come anyway, beta." So I did, in a red kurta with the flower basket. I didn't say the mantras, but I stood beside her while she sang the aarti, and the smell of camphor and marigold took me back to being five. I held her hand. Tenzin, my friend from the hostel, texted, "Weird to go if you don't believe?" I wrote back, "It's not about proving anything. It's about her and me." Ajji whispered afterwards, "You don't have to believe, you just have to be here." I cried a little on the bus. Not sad. Just full. Irawati

qa.q: What did Ajji say when Irawati told her about doubting God last year?
qa.a: Ajji said, "Come anyway, beta."

qa.q: How does Irawati feel at the end of the day?
qa.a: Irawati feels full and moved, not sad. The camphor and marigold smell and holding Ajji's hand bring back childhood warmth.

qa.q: Which choice by Irawati let honesty and belonging sit together?
qa.a: Irawati went to the puja, stood beside Ajji and held her hand without saying the mantras, and was honest that it is about Ajji and Irawati, not about proving anything.

qa.q: How might Ajji have felt having Irawati beside her?
qa.a: Probably happy and reassured. She had invited Irawati anyway and whispered that just being there is enough.

grounding: A non-believer joins a family puja for love and tradition without pretending faith, and stays open about it.

passage:
I stopped believing when I was seventeen. I'm Ganga, and my family knows. But last month, when Nani asked me to sit beside her for the Satyanarayan puja, I said yes.
My cousin Yash raised an eyebrow. "You? At a puja?"
I told him the truth: "I'm not here for the gods. I'm here for Nani."
I sat cross-legged on the floor for two hours. I passed the flowers when the priest asked. I didn't chant the words I don't believe, but I listened to Nani's voice, cracked and certain, and I remembered being five and falling asleep in her lap during this same story.
When the prasad came round, Nani pressed extra into my hand. "I know you don't believe, beti," she said quietly. "I'm happy you came anyway."
I didn't have to pretend. That's what made it feel like home.

qa.q: How long did Ganga sit cross-legged on the floor?
qa.a: Ganga sat cross-legged on the floor for two hours.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling while listening to Nani's voice?
qa.a: She felt nostalgic and tender, remembering falling asleep in Nani's lap during the same story as a child.

qa.q: Why did it matter that Ganga told Yash the truth?
qa.a: Being open, gently, meant she could join the puja out of love without pretending faith, keeping both honesty and belonging.

qa.q: How does Nani seem to see Ganga's presence?
qa.a: Nani seems happy and moved that Ganga came anyway, accepting her disbelief and valuing her company.

grounding: A non-believer attends a family puja out of love, gently open about not believing, and keeps both honesty and belonging.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, Diwali evening.
The students organised the hostel's Lakshmi puja this year. Sachin, 20, second year, is known among the boys for saying openly that he doesn't believe in God, so I was surprised to see him there from four o'clock, arranging diyas along the corridor.
Preeti, from the girls' wing, asked him about it while they were stringing marigolds. I overheard his answer: "I don't pray. But my mother always made rangoli on Diwali, and this is the first year I'm away. I wanted it to look like home." He said it simply, without apology.
During the aarti he stood at the back and didn't join the chants, but he held the plate for the student who led it.
After, he stayed to sweep up the petals. I thanked him. Next step: I've asked him to help plan next year's festivals too.

qa.q: What did Sachin arrange along the corridor?
qa.a: Sachin arranged diyas along the corridor.

qa.q: What might Sachin have been feeling while stringing marigolds?
qa.a: Sachin was probably homesick and nostalgic, missing his mother's Diwali rangoli in his first year away.

qa.q: What in Sachin's behaviour keeps both honesty and belonging?
qa.a: He openly said he doesn't pray, yet helped with love for the tradition, standing respectfully at the back and holding the plate.

qa.q: How might Preeti feel after hearing Sachin's answer?
qa.a: Preeti may feel touched and understand that someone can take part out of love without pretending to believe.

grounding: A warden's note shows a non-believer joining a Diwali puja out of love and memory, gently open about not believing.

passage:
Eid, 6 a.m.
Went to the Eidgah with Abbu and Tanvir this morning, like every year. I haven't prayed properly in two years. They both know. Last year I told Abbu, gently, "I don't believe the way you do, but I want to come."
Today Abbu handed me my old prayer mat anyway. I stood in the women's row with Ammi and my cousins. When they bowed, I stood still, hands folded, and just listened to thousands of people breathing together. It still gives me goosebumps.
Afterwards Tanvir, who is fourteen and dramatic, said, "You didn't even pray, Apa." Ammi said, "She came. That's enough." And then she hugged me longer than usual.
We ate sheer khurma at Nani's and I fed the little cousins. I don't believe, but I belong here. I don't have to lie to have both.
Sharmila

qa.q: What did Abbu hand Sharmila?
qa.a: Abbu handed her old prayer mat to her anyway.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling as she listened to thousands of people breathing together?
qa.a: Sharmila felt awe and a sense of belonging, getting goosebumps even without praying.

qa.q: Why did telling Abbu last year help today?
qa.a: Because Sharmila had gently been open about not believing, she could join the Eid prayer out of love without pretending, and her family accepted it.

qa.q: How does Ammi seem to feel about Sharmila coming?
qa.a: Ammi seems content and loving, saying "She came. That's enough," and hugging her longer than usual.

grounding: A non-believer attends Eid prayers with family for love and tradition, gently open about her disbelief, keeping honesty and belonging together.

passage:
Madhuri: Maa wants you at the Satyanarayan puja on Sunday. you coming?
Madhav: yes, of course. I'll be there by 9
Madhuri: really? you've said you don't believe in any of it
Madhav: I don't. but it's Maa and Baba's day, and Mausi is coming from Patna
Madhuri: won't it feel fake?
Madhav: only if I pretend. I'll sit with everyone, help with the prasad, hand out the plates. I just won't do the aarti myself
Madhuri: Maa might notice 😟
Madhav: I'll tell her beforehand, kindly. "I'm here for you, not for the ritual." she's heard worse from me 😅
Madhuri: true. she'll probably just be happy you came
Madhav: that's the point ❤️

qa.q: What will Madhav help with at the puja?
qa.a: Madhav will help with the prasad and hand out the plates.

qa.a: Madhav feels love for Maa and Baba and wants to belong on their day, while not wanting to pretend.

qa.a: She may feel a little sad about the belief but mostly glad and loved that Madhav came and was honest with her.
